source.title: TC-Net: Detecting Noisy Labels Via Transform Consistency

page_placements.theme: Held-out degradation without an established interpolation result

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper. The title in the text differs from the catalog title: “Transform consistency for learning with noisy labels.”
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses the claim that deep networks memorize noisy training labels as motivation and reports standard-training baseline test accuracy under label noise. It does not measure training error on fully random labels, unstructured inputs, or the other behaviors specified in V1–V6.
record.gate_note: The paper reports standard-training test-accuracy baselines for CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and Clothing1M, plus text describing test-accuracy curves. These outcomes do not establish whether standard networks fit the training labels, so they are recorded under fits_no_version. The paper's proposed transform-consistency method and its ablations are not results of the claim's object itself. The introduction's statement about memorization is background, not a measured result.
record.test_reason: The study uses memorization and clean-first learning to motivate noisy-label mitigation. Its own Standard-baseline results measure held-out test accuracy, not training-label fit or separate learning trajectories for clean and corrupted labels. The reported test-accuracy rise and decline cannot establish V6's learning order.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that transform consistency, small-loss sample selection, and combined offline hard and online soft labels improve noisy-label classification using one trained network. They report state-of-the-art comparative performance across the tested datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies transform-consistency training and sample selection for noisy-label classification, not the original random-label memorization experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard test accuracy decreases across symmetric corruption rates of 20%, 50%, and 80%: 74.32%, 49.98%, and 24.03% on CIFAR-10; 38.15%, 20.58%, and 6.88% on CIFAR-100. Training fit is unreported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Conventional cross-entropy training generalizes worse at higher symmetric label-noise rates in these experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard test accuracy is also reported under asymmetric corruption and natural Clothing1M noise, without training-fit measurements.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Held-out classification performance varies across noise settings and datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Sections III.B.1–2 describe Standard test accuracy rising and subsequently declining in Figures 3–4, interpreting this as clean-first learning followed by noisy-label adaptation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard training exhibits an early generalization peak followed by deterioration on noisy CIFAR datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 reports lower original-versus-flipped prediction divergence for clean samples than noisy samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transform consistency can distinguish clean and corrupted examples in the tested CIFAR-10 settings.

record.problems: The standard-baseline results report test accuracy but not training error. The paper's text describes test-accuracy curves but gives no numeric training-error results.
record.rows_left_out: No other eligible rows identified. Results for the proposed method, its ablations, and alternative transforms measure the paper's method rather than standard networks' random-label fitting.

untested.parts: Near-zero training error and chance test performance under completely random labels, with unchanged architecture and training hyperparameters.
Relative fitting time for true versus random labels and convergence slowdown with increasing corruption.
Training-set fit with shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training-set fit throughout the corruption range and steady test degradation from zero to complete corruption. Only test accuracy at selected intermediate noise rates is reported.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent random-label fitting and whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
Separate measurements showing shared real-data patterns learned before corrupted labels. Test-accuracy curves and the authors' interpretation do not directly measure that sequence.

record.verdict_notes: All recorded numeric values match the supplied tables. No verdict labels are warranted for V1–V6. The authors' memorization interpretation is stronger than the direct evidence supplied by their test-accuracy curves.

versions.untested_parts: No training error or test error on a completely random labeling is reported.
No comparison of training time or convergence time for true versus random labels is reported.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment is reported.
The paper varies label-noise rates and reports test accuracy, but does not report whether training error remains perfect as noise increases.
The paper does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or augmentation prevent fitting random labels, or whether their removal harms true-label generalization.
The paper describes standard training as learning clean samples before adapting to noisy ones, but does not compare learning real versus random labels over training.

relation.reason: Small-loss selection explicitly relies on clean-first learning. The authors interpret Standard test-accuracy trajectories as memorization, but do not directly establish any claim version.

tranche.reason: Uses memorization and clean-first learning to design noisy-label mitigation. Reported test accuracy, selection precision and transform consistency do not measure training-label fit or separate clean/noisy learning trajectories.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv:2103.13872v1 (2021), titled Transform consistency for learning with noisy labels; the pack identifies a 2022 journal article under a different title. All six values match this supplied preprint; equivalence to the journal version is unverified.
